title: Clara Barton Founds a Red Cross Before Her Country Signs the Treaty
dek: In May 1881, after four years of refusals, Clara Barton formed the American Red Cross on the strength of one letter, and the treaty it depended on stalled again.

story.company: American Red Cross (American Association of the Red Cross)
story.event: Forming the American Association of the Red Cross in Washington before the United States had joined the Geneva treaty
story.summary: On 21 May 1881, the day after Secretary of State James Blaine wrote that the Garfield administration would recommend the Geneva treaty to Congress, Clara Barton held a meeting in Washington that formed the American Association of the Red Cross, which elected her president on 9 June. President Garfield was shot on 2 July and the treaty stalled; the first local society formed in Dansville, New York, in August, gave relief after the Michigan forest fires that autumn, and the Senate ratified the treaty on 16 March 1882.
paragraphs: On 20 May 1881 James Blaine, the new Secretary of State, wrote to Clara Barton that President Garfield's administration would ask Congress to adopt the Geneva treaty protecting the war-wounded. Barton, then 59, judged that this warranted action. The next day she held a meeting in Washington that formed the American Association of the Red Cross. The United States had still not signed the treaty.

She had been trying for four years. She had seen the Red Cross at work in Europe during the Franco-Prussian War and came home in 1873, she wrote, more broken than she went, and recovered at a sanitarium in Dansville, New York. She took a letter from the International Committee in Geneva to President Hayes. It was passed to an assistant secretary of state who had seen the treaty refused before. "It would be declined because it had been declined," she later wrote. Rather than invite a third refusal, she waited, tried Congress, and in 1878 published a pamphlet arguing that an American society should also serve in peacetime disasters. When her strength failed she went home, resolved, she wrote, to outlive that administration.

Garfield, inaugurated in March 1881, sent her to Blaine, who kept her waiting an hour, admitted he knew almost nothing of the Red Cross, then heard her out. The society she formed had no standing abroad: the International Committee, remembering an earlier American society left powerless by Washington's refusal, declared it would wait for the treaty before recognising the new one. At a second meeting, on 9 June, Barton was elected president on Garfield's own nomination. She meant, the National Park Service's history says, to hold the office only until the treaty was signed.

On 2 July Garfield was shot; he died on 19 September, and the treaty waited again. In Dansville on 22 August, townspeople formed the first local society, with 57 members. That autumn, when forest fires swept Michigan, the Dansville and Rochester societies sent money and supplies: the Red Cross's first relief work in America, ahead of the treaty. The Senate ratified it on 16 March 1882. Barton wrote in her journal that she had waited so long and "was so weak and broken, I could not even feel glad." She led the Red Cross for 23 years.

quote.text: by acquiescing in the hindrance and by being content to transfer thy efforts to that which is allowed, another opportunity of action is immediately put before thee in place of that which was hindered
quote.source_title: Thoughts of Marcus Aurelius Antoninus, tr. George Long, Project Gutenberg eBook #15877
quote.connection: Marcus Aurelius advises accepting a hindrance and moving one's effort to whatever is still allowed. When the treaty stalled with Garfield's death, Barton did not wait for it: she put her effort into a village society in Dansville and into relief for Michigan, work nobody had to approve.

reflection: Barton's years of waiting were neither idle nor heroic. She was ill for part of them, went home when her strength gave out, and wrote and lectured when she could. When the opening came she had a pamphlet, a letter and friends willing to sit on a board, and she moved the next day.

Some of what you want for your work depends on decisions you do not control: an approval, a budget, someone else changing their mind. Marcus does not ask you to stop wanting those things. He asks you to notice what is allowed this week and put your effort there, so that the waiting also becomes preparation.
invitation: Name one thing you are waiting for someone else to decide. Then write down one piece of work it does not block, and do the first small part of that today.

sources.title: About Clara Barton
sources.supports: Barton learned of the Red Cross in Switzerland in 1869 and worked with it in the Franco-Prussian War; founded the American Red Cross on 21 May 1881; the United States ratified the Geneva Convention by 1882; she was president for 23 years, retiring in 1904; the 1884 'American Amendment' on peacetime disaster relief.

sources.title: Clara Barton (biography by Debra Michals, 2015)

research_notes: Founding date: Barton's own book, the Red Cross, the National Women's History Museum and the Dansville library give 21 May 1881; the National Park Service handbook says 'in June 1881' Barton and friends formed the association, which reflects the 9 June meeting that elected officers. The story gives both meetings. Location: the Dansville library says the first meeting was in Barton's apartment on I Street; a RealClear Public Affairs column says a first meeting on 12 May was at Senator Omar Conger's home; the story says only 'in Washington'. Blaine's letter is dated 20 May 1881 in both Barton books, while Moynier's reply of 13 June refers to a letter of 23 May; the story uses 20 May, and W. E. Barton's statement that the meeting followed 'on the very next day'. Hayes approach: Barton's own account says she presented the Geneva letter to Hayes in 1877; Hayes's note of introduction is dated 4 January 1878 and the NPS handbook says 1878, so the story gives no year for it. 'Trying for four years' counts from 1877; the NPS says she began work as early as 1876. Barton is credited by her cousin W. E. Barton (1922) as almost the sole American advocate; the NPS handbook, by Barton biographer Elizabeth Brown Pryor, is more critical, noting that she unfairly disparaged the earlier advocates Charles Bowles and Henry Bellows; the story does not claim she was the only advocate. The NPS handbook gives $80,000 in money and materials from the Dansville and Rochester chapters for Michigan, while the Dansville library says Dansville collected $300; the story gives no figure. The International Committee's decision to withhold recognition until the treaty was signed is taken from its report reproduced in Barton's book; the story does not claim she knew of it on 21 May. Barton's journal words are quoted from the NPS handbook. The Library of Congress Clara Barton Papers pages returned 403 and are not cited. The Marcus Aurelius passage is a general counsel on hindrances, applied by analogy.
